monitored_sources: CO Division of Real Estate position statements

rules.source: CREC Exclusive Right-to-Buy Listing Contract (BDB24-6-24) §7 compensation blanks; Burnett v. NAR settlement practice changes (eff. 2024-08-17); C.R.S. 12-10-203

payload.summary: Pre-filled buyer-broker fee percentage presented as if standard.

finding.default_analysis: The compensation blank arrives pre-filled with a percentage. Buyer-broker compensation is negotiable and is not set by law or by any MLS rule; the blank could equally hold a flat fee, an hourly rate, or a lower percentage with a cap. Ask what the number would be if you proposed it.

rules.source: CREC BDB24-6-24 §2 brokerage services area blank; CO Division of Real Estate buyer-agency guidance

payload.summary: Agreement scope covers an entire region rather than the search actually underway.

finding.default_analysis: The services-area blank is filled region-wide, obligating the buyer to this broker for ANY purchase anywhere in the territory during the term. The blank could have named one county, one town, or one listing. Region-wide scope plus a backstop clause is how a buyer ends up owing a fee on a property the broker never touched.

payload.summary: Buyer personally backstops the fee if seller-side payment falls through.

all_of: (?:seller|landlord|listing broker(?:age)?)[^.]{0,160}?(?:does not pay|fails? to pay|shall not pay|will not pay)

finding.default_analysis: If the seller or listing brokerage does not pay, the buyer pays the entire unpaid fee at closing — on top of down payment and closing costs. The blank could have capped buyer liability, made the fee contingent on seller-side payment, or struck the backstop entirely. Exposure shown is the pre-filled percentage applied to the configured target price.

rules.source: CREC BDB24-6-24 fee-earned and survival-of-obligations provisions

payload.summary: Fee is earned and survives even when the deal dies on buyer default.

finding.default_analysis: If the buyer defaults on a purchase contract, the broker's fee is still earned, due, and payable — the buyer pays for a closing that never happened, on top of any earnest money already lost. The blank could have limited the fee to transactions that actually close.
